You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

steps.text:
Demo: input has a few stray colored cells (7 at (5,3), 6 at (7,4)). Output replicates pattern: each 7 produces 7's at mirrored positions relative to grid? Let's analyze.

Input stray cells: 7 at row5 col3, 6 at row7 col4.
Output:
row0: 7 5 3 7 5 — 7 at col0 and col3
row2: 5 6 3 5 6 — 6 at col1 and col4
row5: 7 5 3 7 5
row7: 5 6 3 5 6

Grid 9x5. Input 7 at (5,3). Output 7s at (0,0),(0,3),(5,0),(5,3)? row5 col0 is 7 yes. And 6 at (7,4) → 6 at (2,1),(2,4),(7,1),(7,4).

So each stray cell gets copied at positions: (r,c), (r, c'), (r', c), (r', c') where c' = ... For 7: (5,3)→ also (5,0),(0,3),(0,0). c' = 0? cols 3 and 0: maybe c' = W-1-c = 1? No. Hmm cols involved: 0 and 3. Rows: 0 and 5. Maybe relative to the divider lines? The grid has divider rows/cols of color 3: column 2 is all 3, row 4 all 3. So grid divided into 4 quadrants (2x2 blocks). Stray cell in quadrant... 7 at (5,3) is in quadrant row 1 (rows 5-8), col 1 (cols 3-4). Copies appear in all 4 quadrants at same position: quadrant offset + (0,0) of quadrant. (5,3): quadrant (1,1) → copies at (5,0) [quadrant (1,0) pos(0,0)], (0,3) [quad(0,1) pos(0,0)], (0,0). Yes! 6 at (7,4): quadrant (1,1), pos within quadrant (2,1) (rows 5,6,7→index2; cols 3,4→index1). Copies: (7,1),(2,4),(2,1). Matches.

Test grid 20x7. Dividers: rows 6 and 13 all 3; no divider columns? Check columns... column-wise, test has no full-3 column. Hmm demo had both a divider row and column. Test: only divider rows. So horizontal strips only? Rows 0-5, 7-12, 14-19 are 2s. Stray cells:
(14,5)=7, (14,6)=7? Row14: "2 2 2 2 2 5 7" → (14,5)=5,(14,6)=7.
(15,4)=7.
(16,5)=5.
(18,1)=6,(18,2)=5.
(19,1)=6.

But there are 5s too — are 5s also stray, or is 5 the "base" color in demo? Demo base is 5, stray are 7,6. Test base 2, divider 3, strays: 5,6,7. Hmm 5 appears in test too. So strays are 5,6,7.

Replicate in 3 strips: each strip height 6, rows offsets 0,7,14. So copy each stray at same column in all three strips.

Strip row index = r - strip_start. Copies at r+7, r-7, r-14 etc., same column.

Compute:
(14,5)=5 → (0,5),(7,5)
(14,6)=7 → (0,6),(7,6)
(15,4)=7 → (1,4),(8,4)
(16,5)=5 → (2,5),(9,5)
(18,1)=6 → (4,1),(11,1)
(18,2)=5 → (4,2),(11,2)
(19,1)=6 → (5,1),(12,1)

Wait also 5 at (14,5),(16,5),(18,2). Are 5s stray? In demo 5 was base. Here base is 2. So yes 5 is stray. Also 7s. Apply all non-2, non-3.

Output grid: base 2, rows 6 and 13 = 3, plus copies.
